before.content_html:
Why Did Orwell Write Animal Farm?

George Orwell (born Eric Arthur Blair, 1903) was a democratic socialist who believed passionately in equality and freedom. His experience fighting in the Spanish Civil War (1936–39) was pivotal: he witnessed Soviet-backed communists attacking their own allies, showing him that revolutionary ideals could be betrayed by those seeking power. After Spain, Orwell became fiercely opposed to totalitarianism in all its forms.

Key Fact

Orwell wrote Animal Farm (published 1945) specifically to show how Stalin had corrupted the ideals of the Russian Revolution. Crucially, Orwell was NOT attacking socialism itself — he was attacking its corruption under authoritarian rule. This distinction is essential for AO3: Orwell’s target is tyranny, not equality.

Animal Farm is subtitled “A Fairy Story” — deliberately ironic, since the content is anything but light-hearted. Orwell chose the form of a fable to make complex political ideas accessible. By giving human qualities to animals, he could satirise Stalin’s regime without naming it directly, reaching a wider audience than any political essay could.

The Russian Revolution: Essential Background

Before 1917, Russia was ruled by Tsar Nicholas II, who held absolute power over a country where most people lived in extreme poverty. Two revolutions occurred in 1917: in February, protests forced the Tsar to abdicate; in October, the Bolsheviks, led by Vladimir Lenin, seized power. They were inspired by Karl Marx, who argued that the working class should overthrow the ruling class and share wealth equally.

After Lenin’s death in 1924, a power struggle erupted between Leon Trotsky (an intellectual who wanted to spread revolution worldwide) and Joseph Stalin (a pragmatic operator who wanted to consolidate power in Russia). Stalin won. He exiled Trotsky (who was later assassinated in Mexico in 1940) and established a dictatorship characterised by purges, show trials, a secret police (the NKVD) and a cult of personality. This is the precise historical sequence that Animal Farm allegorises: Old Major = Marx/Lenin, Snowball = Trotsky, Napoleon = Stalin.

Propaganda and Control

Stalin maintained power through propaganda — the state newspaper Pravda (meaning “truth”) printed only what the government approved. History was rewritten: Trotsky was erased from photographs. Citizens were encouraged to report “enemies of the state” — even family members. Orwell mirrors this through Squealer, who represents the propaganda machine, and Napoleon’s dogs, who represent the secret police.

Key Fact

Napoleon = Stalin (dictator who seizes power through fear). Snowball = Trotsky (intellectual rival, exiled). Old Major = Marx and Lenin (the revolutionary thinker whose ideas are corrupted). Squealer = Pravda/Soviet propaganda. The dogs = NKVD/secret police. Boxer = the exploited working class.

Allegory, Satire and Fable

Animal Farm combines three literary forms. As an allegory, every element maps onto the Russian Revolution. As a satire, it uses dark comedy to expose the absurdity of totalitarianism — the pigs sleeping in beds then changing the commandment to add “with sheets” is both funny and chilling. As a fable, it delivers a moral lesson through animal characters. Understanding all three forms is essential for OCR.

Orwell struggled to get Animal Farm published. During World War II, the Soviet Union was Britain’s ally against Nazi Germany, and publishers feared offending Stalin. T.S. Eliot at Faber rejected it. It was eventually published in August 1945 — just as the war ended and the Cold War began. The timing was perfect: Britain was beginning to recognise the dangers of Stalinism, and the novella became an instant bestseller.

For OCR Component 01 Section A, this context is essential. Part (a) asks you to compare an extract from Animal Farm with an unseen modern prose extract. Part (b) asks a broader question about the whole text. AO3 (context) requires you to connect Orwell’s choices to the Russian Revolution, his political beliefs and the literary forms he uses.

Key Fact

Orwell was attacking the corruption of revolutionary ideals under Stalin’s totalitarian regime. He was NOT attacking socialism itself — he was a democratic socialist who believed in equality. His target was tyranny masquerading as liberation. This distinction is the most important AO3 point for Animal Farm.

before.content_html:
The Power Struggle: Napoleon vs Snowball

Chapters 4–6 chart Napoleon’s rise to sole power. The central conflict is between Napoleon and Snowball — paralleling the Stalin-Trotsky struggle. Snowball is the intellectual: he designs the windmill, organises committees and debates policy openly. Napoleon is the operator: he says little in public, works behind the scenes and has been secretly training the puppies taken from their mothers in Chapter 3.

Key Fact

Napoleon seizes power by unleashing the dogs (secret police) on Snowball during a meeting, driving him off the farm. He then abolishes debates, creates a committee of pigs to make decisions, and claims the windmill was his idea all along. This parallels Stalin’s exile of Trotsky, his centralisation of power, and his appropriation of Trotsky’s policies after removing him.

The moment Napoleon unleashes the dogs is the novella’s political turning point. Nine enormous dogs, wearing brass-studded collars, chase Snowball off the farm. There is no trial, no vote, no justification until afterwards. This parallels Stalin’s use of the NKVD to eliminate opponents. Violence replaces debate as the mechanism of power.

The Windmill Debate

The windmill debate is crucial. Snowball argues it will reduce the animals’ workload; Napoleon opposes it. After expelling Snowball, Napoleon reverses his position and claims the windmill was always his idea — Squealer explains that Napoleon’s apparent opposition was “tactics.” This Orwellian rewriting of history is one of the novella’s most chilling techniques: the pigs control the past as well as the present.

After Snowball’s expulsion, Squealer works overtime. He tells the animals that Snowball was always a traitor, that he was secretly working with Jones, and that Napoleon’s bravery won the Battle of the Cowshed. The animals are confused but lack the confidence to argue: “If Comrade Napoleon says it, it must be right.” Orwell shows how propaganda works not by convincing people but by confusing them — making them doubt their own memories. This technique, later elaborated in Nineteen Eighty-Four, is one of Orwell’s most enduring insights.

“Napoleon Is Always Right”

Boxer adopts a second motto: “Napoleon is always right.” This is devastating because Boxer is the most admirable character — strong, honest, hardworking and loyal. His unquestioning devotion to Napoleon shows how cult of personality works: it exploits the best qualities in people (trust, loyalty, willingness to sacrifice) for the worst purposes. Boxer’s loyalty will ultimately kill him.

Key Fact

Boxer’s motto shows how totalitarian regimes exploit loyalty. The most hardworking, honest citizens are the most vulnerable because their trust is genuine. Boxer does not question Napoleon because he cannot imagine that someone he trusts would betray him. Orwell shows that the strength of totalitarianism lies not in the tyrant’s power but in the people’s willingness to believe.

The Commandments Begin to Change

In Chapter 6, the pigs move into the farmhouse and sleep in beds. When the other animals check the commandments, they find “No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets.” The addition is Orwell’s satirical masterstroke: the commandments are being rewritten, but so subtly that the animals cannot be sure they are wrong. Their inability to read well enough to challenge the changes mirrors how uneducated populations are vulnerable to manipulation.

The farmhouse represents the privileges of the ruling class. Jones lived there; now the pigs do. By moving into the farmhouse, the pigs have literally taken Jones’s place. The beds represent comfort and luxury that the working animals are denied. Orwell uses the farmhouse to show that the revolution has not created equality — it has simply replaced one set of rulers with another. The physical space of power has not changed; only its occupants have.

These chapters also introduce Napoleon’s trading with neighbouring farms (paralleling the USSR’s economic dealings with capitalist nations) and the rewriting of history regarding the Battle of the Cowshed, where Snowball’s heroism is gradually erased and Napoleon’s role is inflated. Orwell shows that controlling the narrative of the past is essential to maintaining power in the present.

Key Fact

(1) Expels Snowball using the dogs (force). (2) Abolishes debates and creates a committee of pigs (centralisation). (3) Claims the windmill was his idea and rewrites Battle of the Cowshed history (propaganda). Force + centralisation + propaganda = totalitarian control.

before.content_html:
The Purges (Chapter 7)

Chapter 7 is the novella’s darkest moment. Napoleon summons the animals and, with the dogs at his side, demands confessions. Several animals “confess” to working with Snowball and are immediately executed — their throats torn out by the dogs. This parallels Stalin’s Great Purge (1936–38), where millions were arrested, forced to confess to fabricated crimes, and executed or sent to gulags.

Key Fact

The confessions are forced and false — the animals confess to crimes they did not commit because they are terrified of the dogs. This mirrors the Soviet show trials where defendants confessed to absurd charges under torture. Orwell shows that terror does not need to be rational: its purpose is not justice but submission. The surviving animals are silenced not by argument but by fear.

After the executions, the surviving animals huddle together in shock. Clover looks out over the farm and thinks: “these scenes of terror and slaughter were not what they had looked forward to on that night when old Major first stirred them to rebellion.” This is the novella’s most poignant moment — Clover remembers the original vision of equality and sees it utterly destroyed, but she lacks the words or the power to challenge what has happened.

“Beasts of England” Banned

After the executions, Napoleon bans “Beasts of England” and replaces it with a new anthem praising Animal Farm, composed by Minimus. This is symbolically devastating: the revolutionary song that united the animals is erased, replaced by a personality cult anthem. The revolution’s ideals have been replaced by worship of the leader. Orwell shows that totalitarian regimes always destroy the memory of the original revolution because it exposes the gap between promise and reality.

After the executions, the animals check the Sixth Commandment: “No animal shall kill any other animal.” They find it now reads “No animal shall kill any other animal without cause.” The addition of “without cause” retrospectively justifies the massacre. Later, “No animal shall drink alcohol” becomes “No animal shall drink alcohol to excess” after Napoleon gets drunk. Each alteration follows the same pattern: the pigs commit the act first, then change the rule to accommodate it.

The Battle of the Windmill (Chapter 8)

Frederick (representing Hitler) attacks the farm and destroys the windmill with explosives. The animals fight back and “win,” but at enormous cost — the windmill must be rebuilt and many animals are injured. Napoleon proclaims victory and celebrates with the other pigs by getting drunk. This parallels the devastation of the Eastern Front in World War II and Stalin’s propaganda spin on Soviet losses.

Key Fact

The pattern is: (1) pigs commit a forbidden act; (2) animals check the commandment; (3) commandment has been altered to permit the act. This is Orwell’s satirical representation of how totalitarian regimes rewrite laws retroactively. The animals cannot challenge the changes because they can barely read — Orwell shows that education (or lack of it) is a tool of oppression.

Boxer Under Strain

Boxer works harder than ever on the windmill rebuilding, despite his advancing age. He is splitting his hoof and visibly weakening. He still repeats “I will work harder” and “Napoleon is always right,” even as the regime that exploits him becomes more openly tyrannical. His blind loyalty becomes increasingly painful to read — Orwell wants the reader to feel the injustice that Boxer himself cannot see.

By Chapter 8, Napoleon has become a figure of worship. He is called “our Leader, Comrade Napoleon” and credited with every good thing on the farm. A poem praising him is inscribed on the barn wall beside a portrait. He eats from Jones’s china and drinks whisky. The gap between Napoleon and the ordinary animals mirrors the gap between the Soviet elite and ordinary citizens — the revolution that promised equality has produced a new ruling class indistinguishable from the old one.

Orwell’s use of irony intensifies in these chapters. The animals work harder than under Jones, eat less, and live in fear of execution — yet Squealer produces statistics “proving” that food production has increased. The gap between propaganda and reality is the novella’s most bitter joke.

Key Fact

The animals work harder and eat less than under Jones, yet Squealer’s statistics ‘prove’ improvement. The revolution for equality produces a new ruling class. The song of liberation is replaced by a personality cult anthem. Freedom from tyranny produces worse tyranny. Every irony exposes the gap between the revolution’s promises and its reality.

before.content_html:
Boxer’s Death (Chapter 9)

Boxer collapses while working on the windmill. He has worked himself to destruction — the very quality that made him valuable is what kills him. Napoleon announces that Boxer will be sent to a hospital. A van arrives with the words “Horse Slaughterer” painted on its side. Benjamin, who can read, raises the alarm: “They are taking you to your death!” But it is too late. Boxer is sent to the knacker’s.

Key Fact

Boxer represents the loyal, hardworking proletariat who give everything to the revolution. His motto “I will work harder” embodies selfless dedication. Napoleon sells him to the knacker for whisky money. This is Orwell’s most powerful allegorical point: totalitarian regimes use the working class and discard them when they are no longer useful. Boxer’s death shows that loyalty to a corrupt system is rewarded with betrayal.

Squealer announces that Boxer died peacefully in hospital, with Napoleon at his side. He explains away the “Horse Slaughterer” sign by claiming the van had been bought from the knacker and not yet repainted. The animals accept this lie — they want to believe it. Orwell shows that propaganda succeeds partly because its audience is complicit: they choose comforting lies over painful truths.

The Final Chapter: Full Circle

Chapter 10 jumps forward in time. The windmill is built but used to mill corn for profit, not to ease the animals’ workload as Snowball promised. Most of the original revolutionaries are dead. The pigs now walk on two legs, wear clothes and carry whips. The sheep have been taught a new slogan: “Four legs good, two legs better!”

The Seven Commandments have been replaced by a single statement painted on the barn wall: “ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS.” This is Orwell’s most famous line — a paradox that perfectly captures the hypocrisy of totalitarianism. It is the logical endpoint of every small alteration that has come before. The revolution that began with “All animals are equal” has produced its exact opposite.

Pigs and Humans: Indistinguishable

The novella’s final scene shows the pigs entertaining human farmers in the farmhouse. Napoleon announces that the farm will revert to its original name: Manor Farm. The animals look through the window from pig to man, from man to pig: “it was impossible to say which was which.” This is the novella’s devastating final image — the revolution has come full circle. The pigs have become the humans they overthrew.

Key Fact

The final scene shows pigs indistinguishable from humans. Manor Farm’s name is restored. The revolution has produced no real change — one oppressor has been replaced by another. Orwell’s message is that power corrupts regardless of ideology: whether capitalist (Jones) or communist (Napoleon), the ruling class exploits the working class. The cyclical structure suggests this pattern may be inevitable.

The Cyclical Structure

Orwell’s structural choice to end where the story began — with the farm under the same name, ruled by the same kind of tyrant — is profoundly pessimistic. The word “revolution” literally means “turning” — and the farm has turned full circle. This cyclical structure implies that revolutions do not create new worlds; they repeat old patterns.

Some readers argue the ending contains a flicker of hope. The animals see the pigs and humans as identical — they are no longer fooled. Benjamin, the cynical donkey who has watched everything with knowing silence, is still alive. Orwell may be suggesting that awareness, even belated awareness, is the first step towards genuine change. However, the novella offers no mechanism for that change, and Orwell’s tone is deeply pessimistic.

The final chapters force the reader to confront Orwell’s central question: is the corruption of revolutionary ideals inevitable, or can it be prevented? Orwell does not answer definitively, but his structure suggests deep scepticism. The fable form, with its promise of a moral lesson, delivers a lesson that is itself morally ambiguous: beware of all who seek power, even those who promise liberation.

Key Fact

“The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which.” The pigs have become indistinguishable from the humans they overthrew. The revolution has failed. Power has corrupted absolutely.

before.content_html:
The Allegorical Framework

Animal Farm is a sustained allegory of the Russian Revolution and its aftermath. Understanding the allegorical mapping is not optional for OCR — it is the foundation of AO3 context. But sophisticated responses go beyond simple matching to explore why Orwell chose allegory as his form and what it achieves that a straightforward political essay could not.

Key Fact

Allegory: (1) makes complex politics accessible through familiar characters (animals); (2) creates emotional engagement (we care about Boxer in a way we might not care about statistics); (3) achieves universality (the story applies beyond Russia to any revolution corrupted by power). These are AO2 points about Orwell’s choice of form.

The Windmill

The windmill symbolises Soviet industrialisation — Stalin’s Five-Year Plans that promised modernisation but were achieved through forced labour and immense human cost. In the novella, the windmill is built, destroyed, rebuilt and ultimately used to mill corn for profit rather than to ease the animals’ workload. It represents the gap between the revolution’s promises (technology serving the people) and its reality (the people serving technology).

The Seven Commandments

The commandments symbolise the constitution or founding principles of a revolution. Their gradual corruption — each one subtly altered to accommodate the pigs’ behaviour — mirrors how Soviet law was manipulated to serve the ruling elite. Orwell’s structural choice to show the changes after the acts they justify makes the satire devastating: the law follows power, not the other way round.

Moses’s tales of Sugarcandy Mountain — a paradise where “it was Sunday seven days a week, clover was in season all the year round, and lump sugar and linseed cake grew on the hedges” — represent religion’s role in pacifying the oppressed. The animals listen hopefully because their present lives are miserable. Napoleon tolerates Moses because a population focused on the afterlife will not rebel in the present. This parallels Marx’s famous critique of religion as “the opium of the people.”

“Beasts of England”

The revolutionary anthem symbolises the idealism of the revolution itself. Its banning after the purges represents the suppression of revolutionary memory — totalitarian regimes always destroy the original vision because it exposes how far they have fallen. The replacement anthem, praising Napoleon, shows how cultural control serves political power.

Key Fact

The banning of ‘Beasts of England’ symbolises the destruction of revolutionary idealism. The song represented the original dream of equality. Napoleon replaces it with a personality cult anthem because the original song, if remembered, would expose the gap between what was promised and what was delivered. Cultural control is essential to totalitarian power.

The Farmhouse

The farmhouse symbolises the privileges of the ruling class. Jones lived there; now Napoleon does. The animals are forbidden from entering, just as Soviet citizens were excluded from the Kremlin. By moving into the farmhouse, the pigs physically occupy the space of the oppressor they overthrew. The beds, china and whisky are specific symbols of luxury that the revolution was supposed to abolish.

The farm is a microcosm for any society undergoing revolution. Its boundaries create a closed world where Orwell can trace the full arc from rebellion to tyranny. The neighbouring farms represent other nations: Pilkington (England/the West), Frederick (Germany/Hitler). Their shifting alliances with Animal Farm mirror the USSR’s wartime diplomacy, including the Nazi-Soviet Pact and the eventual alliance with the West.

The power of Orwell’s allegory is that it works simultaneously as a specific critique of Soviet history and a universal warning about power. A student who can discuss both levels — the specific (Stalin, Trotsky, the Purges) and the universal (how power corrupts, how propaganda works, how revolutions fail) — will achieve the top band.

Key Fact

The windmill (Soviet industrialisation/false progress), the commandments (corrupted founding principles), Sugarcandy Mountain (religion pacifying the oppressed), ‘Beasts of England’ (revolutionary idealism, suppressed), the farmhouse (ruling-class privilege). For each, explain both the allegorical meaning and Orwell’s wider purpose.

before.content_html:
The Five Key Themes

Every exam question on Animal Farm connects to at least one of these themes. Prepare quotations and analysis for each.

1. Power and Corruption

The central theme. Lord Acton’s maxim — “Power tends to corrupt, and absolute power corrupts absolutely” — is Animal Farm’s thesis. Napoleon’s rise from scheming pig to tyrannical dictator shows how power corrupts regardless of original intentions. The cyclical structure suggests this may be inevitable.

2. Propaganda and Language

Orwell shows that language is the most powerful tool of control. Squealer’s rhetoric, the changing commandments, the sheep’s chanting, the banning of “Beasts of England” — all demonstrate how language shapes thought. Key quotation: Squealer can “turn black into white.”

Key Fact

(1) Squealer’s statistics proving food production has increased (when it hasn’t). (2) The commandments being altered to justify the pigs’ behaviour. (3) The sheep being retrained to chant “Four legs good, two legs better.” Each example shows a different propaganda technique: false data, retroactive law, and mindless repetition.

3. Class and Inequality

The revolution promises equality but produces a new class system: pigs (rulers), dogs (enforcers) and the other animals (workers). The final commandment — “some animals are more equal than others” — encapsulates how class hierarchy reasserts itself even after revolution. Orwell suggests that without structural safeguards, inequality is inevitable.

4. Revolution and Its Failure

Why do revolutions fail? Orwell identifies several factors: the concentration of power in a small elite, the lack of education among the masses, the effectiveness of propaganda, and the willingness of the powerful to use force. The cyclical structure — Manor Farm returning to its original name — suggests that revolution without education and vigilance produces only new oppression.

Education is the key to freedom — or its absence is the key to oppression. The pigs maintain power because they can read and the other animals cannot. The commandments can be changed because most animals cannot verify the originals. Boxer’s inability to learn the alphabet past “D” symbolises the working class’s vulnerability to manipulation. Orwell implies that the most important revolutionary act is education: an educated population cannot be easily deceived.

Key Fact

Power and Corruption (Napoleon’s rise, cyclical structure). Propaganda (Squealer, changing commandments, sheep). Class (new hierarchy: pigs/dogs/workers). Revolution (cyclical failure, Manor Farm restored). Education (literacy as power, Boxer can’t read past D). Prepare quotations for each theme.

Exam Technique for Animal Farm

Comparison task: if your paper pairs an extract from Animal Farm with an unseen prose extract, structure every paragraph as a comparison rather than writing about each text separately. Use linking phrases (“Similarly”/“In contrast”). Analyse language (AO2) and link to context (AO3) throughout.

Extended response: draw on the whole novella. Always discuss both layers: the fable (animal story) and the allegory (Russian Revolution). Embed context throughout. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact question wording and timing guidance.

Key quotations: “All animals are equal” (original commandment). “All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others” (corruption). “Napoleon is always right” (Boxer’s blind loyalty). “Turn black into white” (Squealer’s propaganda). “It was impossible to say which was which” (final line). “I will work harder” (Boxer’s exploitation). “Your lives are miserable, laborious, and short” (Old Major’s rhetoric). Having 8-10 short quotations memorised lets you respond to any question.

Remember: this is a closed-text exam. You cannot take the novella in. Short, embedded quotations are more impressive than long passages. Always connect quotation to technique (AO2) and context (AO3) in every paragraph.

Key Fact

Modern prose is typically assessed through a comparative task paired with an extended response on the whole text, with AO1, AO2 and AO3 all under test. Plan before you write. Every paragraph needs AO1 (response + quotation) + AO2 (analysis of method) + AO3 (context). Check your exam board’s specimen paper for exact timings and mark weightings.

practice_questions.text: ‘Animal Farm suggests that revolution is always doomed to fail.’ How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks:
AO1 (up to 8): Critical response with textual references.
AO2 (up to 8): Analysis of writer’s methods.
AO3 (up to 4): Contextual understanding.
Top band (19-20) Cyclical structure, pigs = humans, Manor Farm restored. BUT Orwell was a socialist who believed in equality — his target is specific corruption, not revolution itself. Both sides.
Upper band (15-18) Thoughtful.
Upper-mid band (11-14) Clear.
Mid band (7-10) Developing.
Lower-mid band (3-6) Simple.
